newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: Dutch KLM buys state-owned shares.
newsitem.headline: Dutch KLM buys state-owned shares.

text.p: Dutch airline KLM said on Thursday it was buying back state-owned shares worth about one billion guilders ($571.4 million) in a move seen as enhancing its appeal to investors and potential partners.

KLM and the Dutch government said in a joint statement they had agreed in principle KLM would buy back some 17.3 million ordinary shares held by the state, so reducing the government's voting stake to 25 percent from the current 38.2 percent.
KLM said the shares would subsequently be withdrawn, reducing its capital base and boosting earnings per share.

"Profits will be divided over a smaller number of shares...and that will have a clearly positive effect of around 20 percent increase in earnings per share," KLM finance director Rob Abrahamsen told reporters.
"We have done a good deal with the government...which gives us the opportunity to privatise further, in line with other European airlines," KLM spokesman Hans Leijte said.
"The deal will bring us closer into line with prevailing market conditions and...so offer us important strategic advantages."

Shattering foreign perceptions of KLM as a state-controlled airline would, for example, stand the carrier in good stead in an upcoming review by U.S authorities of the anti-trust immunity granted to KLM's partnership with Northwest Airlines, Leijte said.
U.S authorities are due to re-evaluate the anti-trust status, granted in 1993, some time next year.

Closer to home, analysts said the deal would make KLM a more attractive alliance partner to non-state owned airlines such as British Airways, currently trying to clinch a link-up with American Airlines.

"The reduction of the state's stake is an ideologically important step," analyst Bert Hoogenhuyze of brokers Amstgeld said. "The U.S. will see the way KLM is headed...that it's definitely not a state dependent like, say, Air France."
"I can see that the division (between state and airline) could be more sharply drawn...Majority state-owned airlines have a bit of a bad name," said Generale Bank's Corne Zandbergen.
However, KLM remained silent on this aspect of the deal, with Leijte saying: "We will make an announcement when we have something to report."

The transaction will be financed from KLM's ample cash reserves. KLM currently has 2.3 billion guilders in cash, and is due a further 0.7 billion guilders from the sale of its Northwest preference shares.
"It's sensible for KLM to do something with their cash pile and this is an effective way of using it given it will boost earnings per share," Zandbergen said.
But other analysts said the fact that KLM was involved in what was essentially an asset management move could be construed as a sign that it lacked strategic imagination.
"In the absence of business style you get asset management," said an analyst who declined to be named.
Gert Jochems, airlines analyst with broker NIB Strating, said he was unhappy at the increase in gearing resulting from the reduction in shareholders' equity.
"Gearing will go back up to 130 percent (from 95 percent) -- I think that's on the high side," he said, adding KLM had always targeted a net debt to equity ratio of less than 100 percent.
But Zandbergen said this was merely a temporary setback in a continuing drive to improve equity ratios.
On the Amsterdam stock exchange KLM shares opened up 1.10 guilders at 46.30 and swiftly rose to 48.60 before settling at around 46.80 in late session.

Under the deal KLM will pay between 900 million and 1.045 billion guilders to the Dutch state. The final price will based on movements in the KLM share price between December 10 and 13, 1996, reduced by a discount of 2.5 percent.
The deal could be shelved if the volume-weighted average of KLM's share price falls below 41.00 guilders or rises above 56.00 guilders during this period.
As a result the airline will not pay more than 49.33 guilders per share, which matches the net equity value per common share recorded on September 30, 1996.
KLM said it was too soon to say when the deal would be finalised, but that an extraordinary shareholders' meeting before the end of the year was unlikely.
The latest payment date has been set for June 1997, but most analysts expect the deal to be rounded off before the start of KLM's 1997/98 financial year starting on April 1.
($1=1.750 Guilder)
